t: If U.S. Senator Baker Were A Woman: An Experimental Study of Candidate Images
abs: About five percent of American political office holders are women. On this indicator of women's status, the United States approximates the worldwide norm (Putnam, 1976). A central research question for those who study women's political roles is why, given the lack of legal or obvious structural barriers to recruitment of female elites, are women still so underrepresented among political officials. The literature on women and politics offers a number of plausible answers.

t: Left-Wing Authoritarianism: Myth or Reality?
abs: Stone (1980) in his paper on The Myth of Left-Wing Authoritarianism attempts to present evidence to the effect that authoritarianism is essentially right-wing, and that although there are some left-wing authoritarians, their number is much smaller than that of right-wing authoritarians. Unfortunately his review of the literature is not as factual or objective as it might be, and his conclusions do not follow from the available data. It may be sufficient to list just a few of the omissions and problems with Stone's paper.

t: The Utility of the Operational Code in Political Forecasting
abs: The study of has evolved as a research focus for the analysis of foreign policy decisions in three stages. Initially, it referred to a focus upon the values, world view, and response repertoire which an individual acquires and shares with other role incumbents in an organization as a result of the organization's recruitment and socialization processes (Merton, 1940). Subsequently, it became a concern for the individual's code of idiosyncratic beliefs concerning the nature of the political universe and the most effective strategies and tactics of political action (Leites, 1951, 1953; George, 1969). Presently, it has evolved into the identification of different types of operational codes as political belief systems whose philosophical and instrumental beliefs vary in an idiographically consistent and nomothetically systematic fashion (George and Holsti, 1975; Holsti, 1977).

t: The "Inherent Bad Faith Model" Reconsidered: Dulles, Kennedy, and Kissinger
abs: It is a reflection of the preparadigmatic state of theory in political psychology that even those studies which are considered to be classics in the field rarely generate follow-on research. One such landmark work is Ole Holsti's (1962) study of the relationship between John Foster Dulles' beliefs and his mode of information processing. Largely as a result of Holsti's analysis, Dulles' name became synonymous with the inherent bad faith model of information processing. Dulles held a closed, negative image of the Soviet Union which he was able to maintain over time by selective attention to new information and by attributional behavior which explained away nonhostile Soviet actions according to the exigencies of weakness.

t: Social Darwinism Reconsidered
abs: The belief that lethal competition is a central and inevitable, even desirable, feature of the human experience may be as old as humanity itself. Though sometimes in abeyance, so far in one way or another it has always recurred eventually, and in the later part of the 19th century became associated with Darwin's work and the authority of science. Within the relevant sciences the credentials of Social Darwinism were soon re-examined and almost unanimously withdrawn. But elsewhere the theme persisted and flourished ideologically. Some believe this contributed much, perhaps even decisively, to the outbreak of the first World War.

t: Conservatism and Misanthropy
abs: acteristically misanthropic, we must also ask what is meant by conservative. Whatever we take conservatism to mean, it is surely something much more than just adherence to the status quo or defense of some orthodoxy. In fact, the origin of the term in British political life was as much abusive as anything else; it was a term of some derision applied to people with a particular set of beliefs. It just happened that the particular constellation of beliefs corresponded fairly closely to what was already considered accepted practice at the time. I would claim, however, that defense of the status quo is not the basic element of what we call a conservative attitude. In fact, there can be circumstances where a conservative advocates change. A strong conservative would, for instance, advocate that we allow private enterprise competitors to the Post Office. Given the steadily worsening service provided by our present postal monopoly, such an innovative step may be the only chance we have to get rid of the present bureaucratic inefficiency.

t: A Discrepancy Measurement of Subjective Political Power
abs: Subjective political power, which is broadly defined as an individual's perceptions of his ability or inability to influence political events, has been studied extensively by social scientists in recent years. It is the thesis of this author that subjective political power and subjective political power discrepancy are conceptually distinct but that this d stinction is often overlooked in studies of political power. The essence of subjective political power is a focus on how much political power one possesses in excess of some minimum amount, whereas the crux of subjective power discrepancy is a focus on the amount of political power one should have but does not possess. Specifically, the former is conceptualized as an individual's focus on how much power he possesses in excess of zero; as thus defined, this concept of power is termed possessed power. The latter is conceived as the discrepancy between the amount of power an individual thinks he should have on a zero-based continuum and has been called deserved power; this concept of power is referred to here as power discrepancy.

The Fall of American Skylab: A Study of Pakistani Students' Reactions
abs: On July 11, 1979, the American Skylab satellite fell on the western part of Australia. However, for a few days before its fall, the parts of the earth on its route generally were tense, nervous, apprehensive, and frightened. Pakistan radio and television had inadvertently suggested that the Skylab might fall anywhere on the Indo-Pakistan-Bangladesh subcontinent. As happens in probable danger situations, the credibility of the radio/television news had increased greatly out of proportion with the expected possibility of the Skylab fall.

t: A Reply to Szasz
abs: Not long ago, for example, Szas reviewed a book on transsexuals and transsexual operations. As a radical libertarian, he should have supported the right of anyone to surgically alter his or her body in any way. Instead, he used the occasion to excoriate psychiatrists for supporting the wishes of transsexuals to change their anatomies. As devoted as his libertarianism is, it was no match for his passion against psychiatry: He had the opportunity to defend the limitless rights of the person, but gave it up to flay the meddling habits of the psychiatrist.

t: The Myth of Id: A Touch of Modernity
abs: The Twentieth Century appears dominated by the Myth of Id, a powerful new Weltanschauung and system of values anchored in desire. Its major characteristics are the worship of instinctual drives, the elevation of subconscious desires to the status of a new god, and the concomitant devaluation of reason, measure, and conscience. This touch of modernity seems to pervade all aspects of individual and social life, as well as culture--broadly understood.
